A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DIRECT and retain the same central algorithm and equivalence proof. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original active-learning experiments on six imbalanced CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN settings, including baseline and parallel-labeling comparisons.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments across additional datasets, training frameworks, and label-noise conditions, with accuracy and minority-class sampling results in the main text and Appendix B.

M1.justification: Both versions use one-vs-rest margin sorting, VReduce threshold identification, and sampling near estimated thresholds. v2 specifies confidence-based tie-breaking where v1 leaves ties unspecified; this adds implementation detail without establishing a changed underlying algorithm. CLIP and FlexMatch introduce evaluation settings rather than a redesigned DIRECT procedure.

E1.justification: v2 retains the six original classification settings and adds ten-class CIFAR-100, binary PathMNIST, FMoW, and iWildcam evaluations. It also adds scenarios with uniformly corrupted annotation labels, substantially extending the evaluated data and annotation conditions beyond v1's noiseless experiments.

E2.justification: The named noiseless ResNet baseline group is retained. v2 additionally evaluates Margin Sampling and CORESET in the LabelBench comparisons, including Figure 14; neither has reported comparison results in v1. BASE is named in both versions, although its curves become visible only in v2.

E3.justification: v2 adds CLIP ViT-B32 evaluation with FlexMatch for noiseless LabelBench experiments and passive training for noisy ones. New protocols include uniform label corruption, 10% label smoothing, and parallel batches of 20. Table 1 also reports 54,448 examples for three-class SVHN, versus 73,257 implied by v1's class counts; whether this reflects changed sampling or a table error is unresolved.

E4.justification: v1 examines parallel labeling but supplies no label-noise robustness experiments. v2 adds a controlled binary CIFAR-100 comparison across 0%, 10%, 15%, and 20% noise, plus broader noisy-label evaluations. Figure 3(f) and Appendix B also add minority-class sampling trajectories to examine the relationship between class balance and accuracy.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports single runs for SIMILAR, BADGE, and BAIT, with four runs for other baselines. v2's Figures 3–5 state that results average four trials with standard-error shading, without those exceptions. This changes reported repetition and uncertainty coverage; the PDFs do not independently establish which experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial accuracy results for new datasets and noisy-label conditions, minority-class count trajectories, and BASE curves absent from v1's Figure 2. Result membership also changes within retained benchmarks: synchronous DIRECT appears for three-class CIFAR-10 in v2 Figure 7, while its binary CIFAR-100 curve from v1 Figure 2(c) is absent from v2 Figure 8. These additions and replacements do not establish same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The Appendix A equivalence lemma and proof are retained. v2 adds an explicit boundary hypothesis and statements about ACED's theoretical guarantees. Definition 4.1 also gains an additional argmax equality that, as printed, subtracts identical class-2 counts and therefore does not express the claimed equivalence.

C1.justification: v2 newly claims the first deep active-learning study addressing simultaneous imbalance and label noise and broadens its contribution to large pretrained-model evaluations. The abstract changes claimed annotation savings from over 15% against state-of-the-art methods and over 90% against random sampling to over 60% and over 80%, respectively. These are revised headline claims across expanded experimental settings.

C2.justification: v2 develops the explanation that maximizing minority-class acquisition can sacrifice informativeness, using DIRECT's lower minority counts than GALAXY to refine the existing balance argument. It also acknowledges slight underperformance on noiseless binary CIFAR-100 and poor FlexMatch behavior under combined imbalance and noise, adding useful qualifications to applicability.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents confidence-based sorting ties, inverse-class-frequency cross-entropy weighting, and details of the CLIP/FlexMatch and label-smoothing setups. However, it removes v1's explicit 500 training epochs and learning rate of 0.01. These are changes in reproducibility information; the newly disclosed weighting does not establish that the retained experiments changed their loss.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially with dedicated discussions of noisy-label active learning and agnostic active learning. v2 distinguishes its setting from label cleaning, weak/strong annotator selection, and heteroskedastic-noise methods, while explicitly connecting VReduce to ACED. These additions support a substantially revised novelty and research-positioning argument.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract and introduction, expands the GALAXY and algorithm explanations, and reorganizes experiments around training frameworks and noise conditions. It adds a conclusion, an impact statement, and a structured results appendix. The narrative revision extends well beyond inserting additional experimental content.

P2.justification: v1's compact six-panel results presentation becomes multiple main-text summaries and an extensive appendix of accuracy and minority-count plot pairs. The explanatory schematic is relabeled and relocated, and Table 1 replaces separate majority/minority counts with total sample counts while adding settings. These constitute substantial changes to visual organization and displays.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important deficiency: v1 claims label-noise tolerance without testing noisy annotations. Section 5.3 and Appendix B.2 provide systematic evidence for that central claim, while additional datasets, CLIP evaluations, and minority-count analyses substantially strengthen empirical scope and explanation. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit training hyperparameters and the erroneous added equality in Equation (1), although those issues weaken reproducibility and mathematical precision.
